unit.title: Coordinate the installation of electrical wiring support system infrastructure

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Before a crew starts putting up cable tray in a new warehouse, what should the coordinator check first?
options: That the tray is the cheapest the supplier has in stock
The drawings, specification and clashes with other services
That the crew have finished every other job on their list
That the painting of the warehouse walls is fully finished

questions.stem: On a hotel project, the plumbers plan to run a large drain pipe along the same ceiling route as your cable tray. What should you do?
options: Raise it at the coordination meeting and agree the routes
Put the tray in first, quickly, so that the route is yours
Run the tray under the drain pipe so they share supports
Leave the tray out and let the cables lie on the ceiling

questions.stem: Which support system is best for many large power cables running a long way across a factory roof space?
options: Small PVC mini-trunking fixed to the roof sheets

questions.stem: Each trapeze hanger carries 1.5 m of tray, and the loaded tray weighs 30 kg per metre. What load does one hanger carry?

options: Plastic wall plugs with short wood screws
Anchors rated for the load, fitted as the maker says

options: Ordinary expanding anchors may not hold in the hollow cores

Fixings in hollow blocks never need to be checked after

Covering the tray so that birds cannot nest in it
Making brackets, frames and trapeze hangers

To raise the earth resistance of the hanger
To stop the threaded rod rusting in damp air
To stop the nuts working loose from vibration

questions.stem: Which tool is best for marking a long, level route for tray brackets along a warehouse wall?

A rotating or line laser level
A tape measure taken up from the uneven floor
A plumb bob hung down from the roof purlins

questions.stem: Why should cable tray bends suit the minimum bending radius of the largest cable on the tray?
options: A bend that is too tight can damage the cable
Tight bends make the tray cheaper to put in
Larger bends stop the tray rusting at its joints
The bend radius sets the tray's earth resistance

options: To let rainwater drain out of the conduit
To fix the conduit to the wall more firmly
To join the conduit's earth to the cable tray
So that cables can be pulled in without damage

questions.stem: The tray route on a drawing is 46 m long, and tray comes in 3 m lengths. Allowing 10% for waste and offcuts, how many lengths should be ordered?
Strut channel costs J$2 400 per 3 m length, and the job needs 12 lengths. What is the cost before GCT?
In a new office building, when are the electrical support systems in the ceiling normally put in?
options: After the ceiling tiles are in, by lifting a few tiles
After the client has moved into the building

options: Flat on the bare ground, so it is easy to pick up

questions.stem: After cutting a length of hot-dip galvanised tray, what should be done to the cut end?
options: Leave it bare, as the zinc will spread over it

questions.stem: Why must the ends of cut steel conduit be reamed before cables are pulled in?
options: To make each length of conduit lighter to carry
So that sharp edges do not cut the insulation
To let the conduit expand freely in hot weather
So that water can drain out of the open ends

questions.stem: Before cables are pulled, what should the coordinator inspect on a finished tray run?
options: Only that the tray has been painted to match
Fixings, level, joints, bonding and clearances
Only how many brackets were used along it
That the tray is all from the same maker

questions.stem: A crew member has fixed tray brackets at 2.5 m spacing, but the specification says 1.5 m. What should the coordinator do?
options: Have the extra brackets fitted before cables go in
Accept it, since the tray is empty and looks fine
Use smaller cables so that the tray stays light
Note it on the as-built drawing and say no more

questions.stem: The architect moves a wall, so the tray route must change. What should the coordinator do?
options: Carry on with the old route and fix it later on
Choose a new route himself and tell nobody about it
Get the change in writing and update the drawings
Stop all work on site until the job is re-tendered

questions.stem: Why are as-built drawings updated as the support systems go in?
options: So the crew are paid for every bracket fitted
So the drawings match the architect's first ideas
So the supplier knows what to deliver next time
So the owner knows where the routes really run

questions.stem: Why is space left above and beside a cable tray?
options: So that birds can roost there instead
To make the tray look smaller from below
For laying cables, heat release and access
To keep the tray away from the light switches

questions.stem: A new tray must run past live busbar trunking in a working factory. What should the coordinator arrange?
options: Let the crew work near it carefully without telling anyone
Cover the busbar trunking with a plastic sheet and carry on
Do the work only at night, when the factory is quiet
A permit, with the busbar isolated and locked off

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the short work plan given to the crew each morning on a large tray job?
options: To record how long each person took for lunch
To set out the day's tasks, areas, materials and hazards
To show the client how much each worker is paid
To list the tools that have gone missing from site

questions.stem: Why should outdoor support systems in Jamaica be fixed more securely than indoor ones?
options: Hurricane winds and rain put large loads on them
Outdoor brackets are made of a weaker metal
Hot sun makes every fixing shrink in its hole
Outdoor runs carry more current than indoor ones

questions.stem: When is cable basket (wire-mesh tray) a good choice?
options: For very heavy power cables over long spans
For outdoor runs exposed to salt spray
For carrying cables through a fire wall
For light data and control cables over a ceiling

questions.stem: Supports for conduit on a flat concrete roof must not damage its waterproofing. What is the best method?
options: Bolt the supports straight through the roof membrane
Use free-standing roof blocks approved for the roof
Lay the conduit loose on the roof with no support
Glue the conduit to the membrane with contact cement

questions.stem: With nothing connected to a supply, how would you check the bonding between tray sections after installation?
options: Low-resistance ohmmeter end to end, leads nulled
Insulation tester between the tray and a cable

questions.stem: Why should agreements made at a site coordination meeting be written down in minutes?
options: So that the meeting lasts a little longer
So that the client pays for the meeting time

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan the installation of cable tray and conduit support systems for a new two-storey office, from reading the drawings to starting work.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the drawings and specification: the routes, the type and size of tray, trunking and conduit, the finishes, the support spacings and the fixings. I walk the site to check the routes and look for clashes with structure, ducts, pipes and sprinklers, and I raise these at the coordination meeting. I take off the quantities: lengths, bends, tees, brackets, hangers, anchors and fire-stopping, adding an allowance for waste, and I order early so materials arrive on time. I plan the order of work with the main contractor, so supports go in after the structure and before ceilings close. I plan access equipment such as mobile scaffolds or a MEWP, and I write a risk assessment and method statement covering work at height, drilling dust, manual handling and any live services nearby. I organise the crew, their tasks and tools, and set out a programme with dates. Finally I brief the crew, set out the first routes with a laser, and check the first brackets before the crew carry on.
markingPoints: Reads drawings and specification; surveys the site
Identifies clashes and agrees them with other trades
Takes off quantities with waste and orders materials
Plans sequence, access, risk assessment and method statement
Organises and briefs the crew, sets out and checks the first work

essays.stem: Explain how you would coordinate the electrical support systems with other trades (plumbing, air-conditioning, ceilings and fire protection) on a hotel project.
essays.modelAnswer: Many trades need the same ceiling space, so coordination must start early. I compare our drawings with those of the plumbing, air-conditioning, fire sprinkler and ceiling trades and mark any places where routes cross or crowd each other. I take these clashes to the site coordination meeting and agree who goes where, usually giving priority to large ducts and drains that need falls, then cable trays, then smaller pipes. I agree heights and clearances, so each trade can install and later maintain its work, and I keep our cables away from hot pipes and below water pipes where possible. I agree the order of installation, so that we do not block each other. I make sure the agreements are written in the minutes and shown on marked-up drawings. On site I check daily that the agreed routes are being followed, and I raise new problems quickly, rather than letting the crew move work on their own. I also tell the ceiling installer where access panels are needed.
markingPoints: Compares drawings and identifies clashes early
Agrees routes, priorities, heights and clearances at coordination meetings
Agrees order of installation between trades
Records agreements in minutes and marked-up drawings
Checks on site and raises new problems promptly; plans access panels

essays.stem: Compare cable ladder, perforated cable tray, cable basket, trunking and conduit. Say where each is best used.
essays.modelAnswer: Cable ladder has two side rails joined by rungs. It is strong over long spans and lets heat escape, so it is best for heavy power cables in factories, plant rooms and risers. Perforated cable tray is a flat sheet with holes and turned-up sides. It supports medium and smaller cables well and is common in plant rooms and ceiling spaces. Cable basket is made from welded wire. It is light, quick to cut and shape, and good for data and control cables above ceilings. Trunking is an enclosed box with a lid. It protects cables and looks neat, so it is used on walls in offices, workshops and classrooms, and it can be divided to keep power and data apart. Conduit is a closed tube, made of PVC or steel. It gives the best protection against damage and the weather, so it is used in walls, in concrete, outdoors and where cables could be knocked. Steel conduit gives more mechanical strength, and PVC resists corrosion.
markingPoints: Cable ladder: heavy cables, long spans
Perforated tray: medium cables, general use
Cable basket: light data and control cables
Trunking: enclosed, neat, can be divided
Conduit: best protection, in walls, concrete and outdoors; steel versus PVC

essays.stem: Explain how Jamaica's coastal air, heat, sun and hurricanes affect the choice and installation of outdoor support systems.
essays.modelAnswer: Near the coast, salt air quickly corrodes plain or lightly coated steel. I would choose hot-dip galvanised or stainless steel tray, brackets and fixings, or a suitable plastic system, and treat cut edges with zinc-rich paint. I would avoid fixing different metals together, such as aluminium on copper, because galvanic corrosion occurs in damp, salty air. Strong sun breaks down ordinary plastics, so PVC conduit and fittings outdoors must be the UV-resistant type. Heat makes PVC expand, so long runs need expansion couplings and fixings that let the conduit slide. Heavy rain means boxes must be weatherproof, with drain holes where the maker allows, and conduit should not let water run into boards. Hurricanes bring strong winds and flying debris, so supports must be closer together, fixed with anchors rated for the load, and cable runs kept close to the building. Roof supports must not damage the waterproofing. After a storm, outdoor systems should be inspected for damage.
markingPoints: Corrosion: galvanised or stainless materials; treat cut edges
Avoids mixing metals (galvanic corrosion)
Sun and heat: UV-resistant PVC and expansion allowance
Rain: weatherproofing and water kept out of boards
Hurricanes: stronger, closer supports and rated anchors; inspection after storms

essays.stem: A tray route is 60 m long with 4 bends. Tray comes in 3 m lengths at J$9 000 each; allow 10% extra for waste. Supports are needed every 1.5 m with one at each end, plus one extra at each bend, at J$1 500 each with 2 anchors at J$150 each. Bends cost J$6 000 each. Work out the quantities and the cost before GCT. Show your working.
essays.modelAnswer: Tray: 60 m ÷ 3 m = 20 lengths. Add 10% for waste: 20 × 1.1 = 22 lengths. Cost = 22 × J$9 000 = J$198 000. Supports: 60 m ÷ 1.5 m = 40 spans, so 41 supports, plus 4 extra at the bends = 45 supports. Cost = 45 × J$1 500 = J$67 500. Anchors: 45 × 2 = 90 anchors. Cost = 90 × J$150 = J$13 500. Bends: 4 × J$6 000 = J$24 000. Total before GCT = J$198 000 + J$67 500 + J$13 500 + J$24 000 = J$303 000. GCT is then added at the current rate. I would also check the supplier's prices and delivery time and allow for labour, access equipment and fire-stopping, which are not included here.
markingPoints: Tray: 22 lengths, J$198 000
Supports: 45, J$67 500
Anchors: 90, J$13 500
Bends: J$24 000; total J$303 000 before GCT
Notes that GCT, labour and other items are added

essays.stem: Explain the hazards of installing support systems at height in an existing, occupied building, and the controls you would put in place.
essays.modelAnswer: The main hazard is falling from height, so I choose the right access: a mobile scaffold with guard rails and locked wheels, or a MEWP used only by trained operators, and stepladders only for short, light tasks. Falling objects can hit people below, so I barrier off the area under the work, use tool lanyards and keep the platform tidy. Drilling into concrete makes silica dust and noise, so we use dust extraction, masks, eye and ear protection, and we warn the occupants. Hidden live cables, water pipes and gas pipes may be in the slab or walls, so I check drawings and use a cable detector before drilling. Existing live equipment, such as busbars or lighting circuits, may be near the route: we isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead with a tester checked before and after, or get a permit and keep safe distances. Manual handling of tray lengths needs two people. Hot weather can cause heat stress, so we drink water and take breaks in the shade.
markingPoints: Falls from height: right access equipment, trained users
Falling objects: barriers, lanyards, tidy platforms
Dust and noise: extraction and PPE; warn occupants
Hidden and nearby services: detection, safe isolation or permit
Manual handling and heat stress controls

essays.stem: Describe the inspections you would carry out on a completed support system before cables are installed, and how you would record them.
essays.modelAnswer: I walk the whole route with the drawings and specification. I check that the route, heights and clearances match what was agreed, and that it does not clash with other services. I check that supports are at the right spacing, square and level, and that every fixing is the correct type, fully tightened and locked where needed. I look at joints and couplers to make sure they are bolted and aligned, with no sharp edges or burrs that could damage cables, and that bends suit the cable bending radius. I check the bonding of metal sections where required and test it with a low-resistance ohmmeter. I check that cut edges on galvanised parts are painted, that outdoor items are the right finish, and that expansion couplings are fitted on long PVC runs. I check fire-stopping is planned at fire walls. I record each item on an inspection checklist, with photos of any defects, and put defects on a snag list with who will fix them and by when. I sign off only when all snags are cleared.
markingPoints: Checks route, heights and clearances against drawings
Checks support spacing, level and fixings
Checks joints, burrs and bend radius
Checks bonding (tested), finishes, expansion and fire-stopping
Records on a checklist with photos and a snag list; signs off when cleared

essays.stem: Explain why metal support systems are bonded to earth where the specification requires it, and how you would make and check the bonding.
essays.modelAnswer: Metal tray, trunking and conduit can become live if a cable's insulation is damaged and a line conductor touches the metal. If the metal is bonded to earth, the fault current flows back through the earth path and the protective device trips quickly, so nobody gets a shock from the metal. Where the specification requires bonding, I make sure each section is joined to the next with the maker's couplers or with bonding links or straps across each joint, especially across painted or expansion joints. Contact surfaces are cleaned of paint and dirt, and the bolts are tightened with the right washers. The system is connected to the main earthing terminal or the board's earth bar with a conductor of the specified size. To check it, with no supply connected, I use a low-resistance ohmmeter with its leads nulled. I measure from the earth bar to the far end of each run, and across joints. The readings should be low and steady. I record them and fix any high reading.
markingPoints: Explains why bonding is needed (fault current, trip, no shock)
Joins each section with couplers or bonding links, especially at painted or expansion joints
Clean contact surfaces, correct tightening; connected to the main earthing terminal
Tests with a low-resistance ohmmeter, leads nulled
Records readings and corrects high ones

essays.stem: A crew member has installed a run of tray at the wrong height, so it will clash with an air duct that goes in next week. Explain how you would deal with this and stop it happening again.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop any more work on that run, so the problem does not grow, and I check the drawings and the minutes of the coordination meeting to confirm the agreed height. I talk to the crew member calmly and privately to find out why it happened: perhaps he had an old drawing, the setting-out mark was wrong, or he was not told about the agreed change. I tell the air-conditioning contractor early, in case a small change to either route would solve it. If not, I plan the correction: the tray is taken down and refixed at the right height before any cables go in, and I record the time and materials used. To stop it happening again, I make sure only the latest drawings are on site and old ones are marked superseded. I set out heights with a laser and mark datum lines myself or check them before work starts. At the toolbox talk I explain the agreed heights for each area. I check the first brackets on each new run before the crew carry on.
markingPoints: Stops work and confirms the correct height from drawings and minutes
Finds the reason without blame
Talks to the other trade early to look for the best solution
Corrects the work before cables go in, and records it
Prevention: control of drawings, setting out, briefing and early checks

essays.stem: Describe how you would supervise a crew of four on a week-long support system installation, including daily planning, quality checks and progress reporting.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the week starts I break the job into areas and tasks and set targets for each day, for example 40 m of tray on the first floor by Tuesday. Each morning I hold a short briefing: the day's tasks and who does each, the materials and access equipment needed, and the hazards and controls, such as work at height and drilling dust. I make sure materials are on hand so the crew do not wait. During the day I check the first brackets of each run for height, level and spacing, and I make spot checks later, correcting problems quickly and showing the right method. I pair less experienced workers with experienced ones. At the end of each day I compare progress with the plan, update the marked-up drawings and note any problems such as clashes or late deliveries. I send a short progress report to the project supervisor, with photos, work done, problems and what is needed. At the end of the week I carry out the full inspection and snag list.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into daily targets
Daily briefing on tasks, materials and hazards
Checks quality early and during the day, coaching the crew
Tracks progress and updates drawings
Reports progress and problems to the supervisor; final inspection and snag list

practical1.title: Plan, estimate and set out a support system route from drawings
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a drawing of a training wall and ceiling bay at the Centre, showing a run of cable tray, a length of trunking and a PVC conduit route to an outdoor box, with the specification (support spacing, finishes, space factor) and a price list in J$. As a group, survey the bay and mark on the drawing any clashes, such as a pipe, a light fitting or a door. Agree how to deal with each clash, as you would at a coordination meeting, and record it in short minutes. Each member then leads one part of the planning: the material take-off (lengths, bends, supports, anchors, fire-stopping and a waste allowance); the cost estimate before GCT; a bar-chart programme for a crew of four; and a risk assessment for the installation. Finally, set out the route on the training wall with a laser level and chalk line, marking every bracket position at the specified spacing, and check another member's marks with a tape.
materials: Drawing of the training bay, specification and J$ price list (from the assessor)
Line laser or rotating laser level, chalk line, tape measures and pencils
Cable detector for checking the wall before marking fixings
Take-off sheet, estimate sheet, programme sheet, risk assessment form and minutes sheet
Calculators, safety glasses and platform steps
photos: The drawing marked up with clashes and agreed changes
The minutes of the group's coordination discussion
The completed take-off and cost estimate
The bar-chart programme and risk assessment
The laser line and chalk line on the wall
The marked bracket positions with a tape showing the spacing
checklist: Found at least one clash and proposed a workable solution
Led their part of the planning accurately
Used the specification correctly (spacing, finishes, fill)
Worked out quantities and costs correctly, including waste
Checked the wall with the cable detector before marking fixings
Set out level and accurate marks with the laser and chalk line
Checked another member's work and recorded corrections
safety: Use platform steps, not chairs or boxes, to reach high marks
Do not look into the laser beam or point it at others
Check walls for hidden cables and pipes before marking fixing points
Keep the floor clear of tools and tapes

practical2.title: Install, bond and inspect a support system run on a training frame
practical2.brief: Using the group's set-out from the assessor's drawing (or a set-out the assessor provides), install on the Centre's training wall and ceiling frame: a run of cable tray on strut brackets with one bend, a trapeze hanger from the frame, a length of trunking with a divider, a PVC conduit run with an expansion coupling and a short steel conduit drop with reamed ends. Give each member a section to install and lead, with the others helping and checking. Before drilling, check for hidden services. Bond the tray sections and the steel conduit as the specification says, then test the bonding end to end with a low-resistance ohmmeter (nothing is connected to any supply). Treat any cut galvanised edges. Then inspect the whole system against an inspection checklist: route, level, spacing, fixings, joints, burrs, bend radius, bonding, finishes and clearances. Write a snag list, fix the snags, and mark the as-built changes on the drawing.
materials: Cable tray lengths, a bend, couplers and bonding links
Strut channel, threaded rod, nuts, lock nuts and washers, brackets and suitable anchors
Trunking with divider and lid; PVC conduit, saddles and an expansion coupling; steel conduit, couplers and a reamer
SDS drill with dust extraction, hacksaw, file, spanners and a torque wrench if available
Laser level, spirit level and tape measure; cable detector
Inspection checklist, snag list and the drawing for as-built marks
photos: The trapeze hanger with lock nuts fitted
The PVC expansion coupling and the reamed end of the steel conduit
The bonding links across tray joints
The bonding continuity test in progress, with the reading
The completed inspection checklist and snag list
The finished system and the as-built drawing
checklist: Checked for hidden services before drilling
Installed their section level, at the specified spacing and with correct fixings
Cut and deburred material, and treated cut galvanised edges
Fitted bonding correctly and helped test it with the leads nulled
